An irrigation system includes a valve configured to control the flow of water through a sprinkler head and a flow sensor configured to measure the water flow rate through the sprinkler head. In some embodiments, the valve is adjusted until the flow sensor measures a water flow rate that matches a first predetermined water flow rate, thereby establishing a first valve position. The valve opening is then adjusted again, either by a set amount or until the flow sensor measures a water flow rate that matches a second predetermined water flow rate, thereby establishing a second valve position.

The first and second predetermined water flow rates each correspond to a throw distance traveled by the water stream discharged from the sprinkler head. The relationship between water flow rate and throw distance is based on empirical data for the sprinkler. A second equation, which relates valve opening to water flow rate for a given pressure, is then used to estimate the effective water pressure. In some embodiments, the first and second valve positions and the first and second water flow rates are used to estimate the effective pressure using the second equation.
outputs.L2: An irrigation arrangement has a valve for regulating water passing through a sprinkler head and a flow sensor for determining the rate of that water flow. In certain implementations, the valve is moved until the sensor detects a flow rate equal to a first preset flow value; the valve setting at that point is identified as a first valve position. The valve is then changed again, either by a specified increment or until the sensor detects a flow rate equal to a second preset flow value; that setting is identified as a second valve position. Each of the two preset flow rates is associated with a corresponding throw distance for the stream of water emitted by the sprinkler head. The association between flow rate and throw distance is derived from empirical sprinkler data. A further equation, which describes the relationship between valve opening and flow rate at a particular pressure, is used to estimate the effective water pressure. In some versions, the effective pressure is estimated from the first and second valve positions together with the first and second water flow rates by applying that further equation.
outputs.L3:
An irrigation system may control and evaluate water delivery by using a valve positioned upstream of a sprinkler head and a flow sensor configured to measure the rate at which water passes through the sprinkler. The valve regulates the amount of water supplied to the sprinkler head, while the flow sensor provides feedback indicating the actual flow rate produced under the current valve setting.

During operation or calibration, the valve is first adjusted until the flow sensor indicates that the measured flow rate matches a first predetermined flow rate. Once this condition is reached, the corresponding valve setting is recorded as a first valve position. This first predetermined flow rate may be selected to produce a known sprinkler performance characteristic, such as a particular throw distance.

The valve is then adjusted a second time. This adjustment may be made by moving the valve by a known or predetermined amount from the first valve position, or by continuing to adjust the valve until the measured flow rate matches a second predetermined flow rate. When the second condition is reached, the corresponding valve setting is recorded as a second valve position. The second predetermined flow rate may likewise correspond to another known sprinkler throw distance.

The predetermined flow rates are selected based on empirical data that relates sprinkler flow rate to sprinkler throw distance. For example, testing may establish that a certain flow rate produces a particular radius or distance of water distribution for a given sprinkler head. By using such empirical relationships, the system can associate measured flow rates with expected irrigation coverage.

After the first and second valve positions and their corresponding flow rates have been established, the system uses this information to estimate the effective water pressure available at the sprinkler. In particular, the system applies an equation or model that relates valve opening to flow rate, taking into account the recorded valve positions and measured or predetermined flow rates. By comparing how the flow rate changes between the two valve positions, the system can infer the effective pressure driving water through the sprinkler head. This estimated pressure may then be used to improve irrigation control, verify sprinkler performance, or adjust watering schedules to achieve desired coverage.
outputs.L4:
An irrigation system may be configured to automatically calibrate and control the performance of one or more sprinklers by using a controllable valve in combination with a flow sensor. During a calibration procedure, the system adjusts the valve to produce selected or predetermined flow rates through the sprinkler. These flow rates may correspond to empirically determined sprinkler throw distances, such as distances measured or characterized in advance for a particular sprinkler type, nozzle, or irrigation zone. By progressively opening or closing the valve and monitoring the resulting flow with the flow sensor, the controller can identify valve positions that produce desired flow conditions.

For example, a sprinkler may be known to achieve particular throw distances at particular flow rates. The controller can use this relationship to set the valve so that the sprinkler delivers water at a flow rate associated with a target throw distance. The system may store the resulting valve positions, measured flow rates, and corresponding sprinkler performance data in memory. This stored calibration information can later be used to operate the sprinkler more accurately under varying conditions, such as changes in supply pressure, zone configuration, or the number of active irrigation devices.

The calibration data may also be used to estimate an effective water pressure at the sprinkler or within the irrigation zone. Because sprinkler flow, valve position, and throw distance are related to operating pressure, the system can infer pressure conditions from the measured flow rates and the valve settings required to achieve them. This pressure estimate may be used even when a dedicated pressure sensor is not installed at the sprinkler. As a result, the system can compensate for pressure variations and more precisely control sprinkler operation.

In use, the irrigation controller may compare a desired sprinkler performance characteristic, such as a target throw radius or application rate, with the stored calibration data. The controller may then adjust the valve to the corresponding position or may dynamically regulate the valve based on real-time flow measurements. If the measured flow deviates from the expected value, the controller can further adjust the valve or update its estimate of effective pressure. This allows the system to maintain consistent sprinkler coverage and water distribution despite changes in hydraulic conditions.

By combining empirical sprinkler performance data with measured flow and controllable valve positioning, the irrigation system provides improved control over sprinkler output. The system can reduce under-watering and over-watering, improve uniformity of coverage, and adapt operation to actual field conditions. In this manner, the irrigation system enables more accurate calibration of sprinkler flow and more precise management of irrigation performance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize this patent disclosure in plain English: an irrigation sprinkler system uses a valve, flow sensor, predetermined flow rates tied to throw distances, and valve-position/flow equations to estimate effective water pressure.
counterfactuals.output:
This patent describes a sprinkler irrigation system that can estimate the water pressure available at a sprinkler without using a dedicated pressure sensor.

In plain English:

- The system has a controllable valve and a flow sensor.
- Each sprinkler or sprinkler setting has known expected flow rates that correspond to different spray distances, or “throw” distances.
- The controller opens or adjusts the valve and measures how much water is flowing.
- It also knows the valve position and uses equations that relate valve opening, water flow, and pressure.
- By comparing the measured flow to the expected flow values and applying those valve/flow formulas, the system estimates the effective water pressure being delivered to the sprinkler.
- That estimated pressure can then be used to determine whether the sprinkler is operating properly, adjust watering performance, or infer the actual spray distance.

The main idea is to use flow measurements plus valve-position modeling to calculate sprinkler pressure indirectly, rather than measuring pressure directly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise technical abstract describing an irrigation system that calibrates sprinkler throw distance by adjusting a valve to first and second flow rates and estimating effective pressure from valve positions.
counterfactuals.output: A sprinkler irrigation system is configured to calibrate throw distance by controllably adjusting a flow-regulating valve between first and second valve positions corresponding to first and second flow rates. During calibration, the system measures or infers the valve positions required to achieve the selected flow rates and estimates an effective sprinkler pressure based on a valve-position-to-pressure relationship, optionally accounting for supply conditions and hydraulic losses. The estimated effective pressure is used to determine or update a throw-distance model for the sprinkler, enabling accurate control of irrigated area without requiring a dedicated pressure sensor at the sprinkler head. The calibrated model may then be used during irrigation scheduling to select valve settings that provide a desired coverage radius while improving water distribution uniformity and reducing overspray.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain an invention where a sprinkler head has a controllable valve and flow sensor, uses empirical flow-rate-to-throw-distance data, and estimates effective pressure from two valve openings.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention is a “smart” irrigation sprinkler head that can measure and control its own water output and infer the pressure available at the head without needing a separate pressure sensor.

It combines three main features:

1. **A controllable valve in the sprinkler head**  
   The sprinkler head includes an adjustable valve, such as an electronically controlled valve, that can be opened to different known positions. By changing the valve opening, the system can regulate how much water flows through the sprinkler.

2. **A flow sensor**  
   A flow sensor measures the actual water flow rate through the sprinkler head. This lets the controller know how much water is being discharged at each valve position, rather than relying only on assumptions.

3. **Stored empirical flow-to-throw data**  
   The system has stored calibration data that relates sprinkler flow rate to throw distance — that is, how far the sprinkler projects water. This data is empirical, meaning it is based on measured performance of the sprinkler rather than purely theoretical calculations.

The invention can determine the sprinkler’s throw distance by measuring flow rate and looking up, or interpolating from, the stored empirical data. For example, if testing shows that a certain nozzle throws water 20 feet at 2 gallons per minute and 25 feet at 3 gallons per minute, the controller can estimate the current throw distance from the measured flow.

A key part of the invention is estimating **effective pressure** at the sprinkler head. Instead of using a pressure sensor, the controller measures flow at two different valve openings. Because the valve positions are known and the flow rates are measured, the system can infer the pressure driving the flow. In simplified terms, flow through a valve depends on both the valve opening and the pressure difference across it. By observing two flow rates at two known valve settings, the controller can solve or estimate the effective pressure available to the sprinkler.

Once effective pressure and throw distance are known or estimated, the sprinkler can adjust operation more intelligently. It may change valve position to achieve a desired throw distance, compensate for pressure fluctuations, improve watering uniformity, reduce overspray, or verify that the sprinkler is performing as expected.

In short, the invention is an intelligent sprinkler head that uses a controllable valve, a flow sensor, and stored empirical performance data to estimate spray distance and effective pressure, allowing more accurate and adaptive irrigation control.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style summary for a smart irrigation sprinkler that adjusts valve opening until measured flow matches predetermined rates corresponding to water stream travel distances, then calculates effective pressure.
counterfactuals.output:
## Summary

A smart irrigation sprinkler is disclosed that automatically regulates water discharge to achieve a selected irrigation throw distance and determines an effective operating pressure based on the regulated flow. In one embodiment, the sprinkler includes a sprinkler body having an inlet, an outlet nozzle, a controllable valve disposed between the inlet and the outlet nozzle, a flow sensor configured to measure water flow through the sprinkler, and a controller operatively coupled to the controllable valve and the flow sensor.

The controller stores or accesses predetermined flow-rate values associated with corresponding water stream travel distances. In response to a selected or commanded travel distance, the controller identifies a target flow rate corresponding to the selected travel distance. During operation, the controller actuates the controllable valve to vary a valve opening and repeatedly compares the measured flow rate with the target flow rate. The controller increases or decreases the valve opening until the measured flow rate substantially matches the predetermined target flow rate for the selected travel distance.

Once the measured flow rate reaches the target flow rate, the controller calculates an effective pressure of the sprinkler. The effective pressure may be calculated using the measured flow rate, a known nozzle characteristic, an orifice coefficient, nozzle geometry, or a stored flow-pressure relationship for the sprinkler nozzle. The calculated effective pressure may be used for monitoring irrigation performance, detecting abnormal supply conditions, identifying clogged or worn nozzles, compensating for pressure variation across an irrigation zone, or communicating system status to an irrigation controller or remote device.

In some embodiments, the predetermined flow-rate values are stored in a lookup table that correlates flow rate with stream travel distance for one or more nozzle types. The controller may receive nozzle identification information, select a corresponding flow-distance profile, and regulate the valve according to the selected profile. The sprinkler may further include wireless or wired communication circuitry for receiving irrigation commands, reporting measured flow and calculated pressure, and coordinating operation with other sprinklers in an irrigation system.

By adjusting valve opening based on measured flow rather than relying solely on supply pressure, the sprinkler can maintain desired stream travel distances under varying water supply conditions. The sprinkler may therefore improve irrigation uniformity, reduce overspray or underspray, and provide pressure-related diagnostic information without requiring a separate pressure sensor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output: An irrigation controller uses two known valve positions, each linked to a measured flow rate or sprinkler throw distance, as reference points. It then uses that estimate to determine the sprinkler’s effective operating pressure.
